1:
The voice from the whirlwind opens a second gallery of untamed things, and its first question — "Knowest thou the time when the wild goats of the rock bring forth?" — sets the movement of the whole speech, for God will humble Job by the very creatures he can neither govern nor so much as observe. The reformed John Gill explains the name: the wild goats are so called because they dwell among the rocks and run upon them, and though their heads are loaded with a vast burden of horns, they so poise themselves that, with the greatest swiftness, they leap from mountain to mountain, as Pliny reports. If, as Olympiodorus asserts, they bring forth their young in the rocks, it is no wonder the time of their bringing forth should be unknown to men, to whom the crags they range are inaccessible.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fills in the natural history and the point of the riddle. The word for wild goat, yael, comes from a root meaning to ascend, for there is no crag so high or steep but this ibex will mount it in a series of leaps; it is native to Arabia, of amazing strength and agility, and goes five months with young, while the hind, the female of the stag, goes eight. To know the mere time, Clarke insists, would be easy and unremarkable; the force of the question lies in the circumstances that bear the print of providence — Pliny's report that the hind with young is guided by instinct to the herb seselis, which eases her delivery, and the stranger fact that thunder, which looks like the more immediate hand of God, has the same effect, so that the psalmist can say "the voice of the LORD maketh the hinds to calve."

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the theology of the panel. God here shows Job what little acquaintance he has with the untamed creatures that run wild in the deserts and live at large, yet are the care of divine providence; for as every individual is fed, so every species is preserved, and, for aught we know, none has gone extinct to this day. Man is wholly ignorant of the time they bring forth — shall we pretend to tell what is in the womb of providence, who cannot tell the pregnancy of a hind? And Henry draws a tender application from the difficulty of their calving, which the next verse will trace: if God helps even the wild hinds to bring forth their young without any aid from man, shall he not much more succour and save in childbearing the women who are his own children in covenant with him? The three voices do not divide; together they make the wild goat's secret birth a first proof that the world runs by a wisdom Job never supplied.
2:
The interrogation presses on from the fact of the birth to its exact reckoning, God asking whether Job can "number the months that they fulfil" and mark the hour of their delivery. The reformed John Gill takes the question of both the wild goats and the hinds, and confesses the gaps in the naturalists' knowledge: the common goat fulfils five months, conceiving in November and bringing forth in March, as Pliny observed, but how many months the wild goats of the rock fulfil no writer he knows has recorded; the hind, by the same authority, goes eight. The precision God demands is a precision no man possesses.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the strophe and weigh its wording: "Observest thou the circles of the hinds? Dost thou number the months which they fulfil, and knowest thou the time of their bringing forth?" The strophe, they explain, treats of the female chamois or steinbocks, the ibices, together with the stags; the name yelim is formed from a root meaning to mount, so that the creatures are literally rock-climbers. The verb they render "observe" is the same used of watching the wind in Eccl. 11:4 and of Eli watching Hannah's mouth in 1 Sam. 1:12; and the infinitive behind "circles" or "travail" carries the sense of bringing forth with pangs, the very throes the next verse will describe. They note too the full spelling of "number" and the euphonic ending on "their bringing forth," small marks of the text's careful hand.

Beneath the grammar the two witnesses agree on the drift of the divine argument, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment gathers verses one and two together, states it plainly: man is wholly ignorant of the time these creatures bring forth, and cannot so much as tell the months of a wild goat's pregnancy. The question is not idle curiosity but a sounding of Job's ignorance; the God who keeps the calendar of every hind's womb, counting the months that Job cannot count, is showing how far the ordering of life runs past the reach of the man who had presumed to reason with him. Gill's tally of the naturalists and Keil and Delitzsch's philology converge on the same confession — that the secret arithmetic of birth belongs to God, who alone observes the circles the wild creatures fulfil and knows the appointed hour none of them can hasten or delay.
3:
The speech follows the wild mothers into their travail, and the witnesses attend to the crouch and the pang the verse compresses into a line. The reformed John Gill reads "they bow themselves" of the posture the creatures take to bring forth their young with greater ease and safety; for the hinds, he notes, bear with great difficulty, and nature has provided helps against it. Thunder, observed before, causes them to bring forth the sooner; the herb seselis they feed on before the birth makes it the easier; and another herb, aros, they use afterward to ease their later pains. The whole is a hidden apparatus of mercy, tending a birth no shepherd oversees.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the movement of the verse in three quick strokes — "They bow down, they let their young break through, they cast off their pains" — catching the sudden violence of the delivery and the throwing off of the birth-pangs as the young are freed. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that "they bow themselves" describes the crouch by which they bring forth, but parts from the others over the closing image: the word rendered "sorrows," chebleyhem, he takes not of the pains but of the afterbirth — the placenta, or the umbilical cord — which the creatures cast out with the young, a sense he says the word has been understood to bear. So a small difference runs beneath the verse: whether the hind casts off her pangs, as Gill, Henry, and Keil and Delitzsch read it, or casts out the afterbirth, as Clarke prefers.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, still expounding the panel of the wild goats and hinds, draws the pastoral comfort the image invites. Though these creatures bring forth their young with a great deal of difficulty and sorrow, and have no assistance from man, yet by the good providence of God their young ones are safely produced and their sorrows cast out and forgotten. Some think it intimated in Ps. 29:9 that God by thunder helps the hinds to calve; and let it be observed, for the comfort of women in labour, that if God helps even the wild hinds to bring forth their young, much more will he succour and save in childbearing those who are his children in covenant with him. The witnesses do not divide over the wonder; whether the hind casts off pang or afterbirth, all read the verse as a window into the tender, unseen providence that carries the desert's births safely through, and that stands nearer still to the daughters of men.
4:
From the birth the speech turns to the weaning and the parting, tracing the fawns until they leave the dam for good. The reformed John Gill reads "their young ones are in good liking" of the plump, fat, and sleek condition of the fawns, thriving under a providence that asks no help from man. The wesleyan-arminian voices fill in the growth and the departure. Adam Clarke explains that after the fawns have sucked awhile the dam leads them out to pasture, where they feed on herbage but not on grain, for they are not born before harvest-time in Arabia and Palestine; so the word bar, here rendered "corn," should rather be "the open field" or country. Following Houbigant and Mr. Good, he reads the sequel as a picture of swift independence: in a short time the young become independent of the mother, "grow up in the fields, and once departing, return to them no more." John Wesley keeps the softer rendering — they grow up "as with corn," that is, as if they were fed with grain — and grounds their going forth in providence: notwithstanding the great weakness caused by their hard entrance into the world, they thrive and then leave, finding sufficient provision abroad by the care of God.

The grammatical-historical witnesses divide with them over the single disputed word. Charles Ellicott glosses "they grow up with corn" but judges it "more probably, perhaps, in the open field, as the word means according to some"; Keil and Delitzsch render the whole strophe to the same effect — "their young ones gain strength, grow up in the desert, they run away and do not return" — making the wilderness, not the cornfield, their nursery. So a genuine, if small, difference of reading stands in the verse: whether the fawns grow as though fed with corn, as Gill and Wesley take it, or grow up in the open field and the desert, as Clarke, Ellicott, and Keil and Delitzsch prefer.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry closes the panel with a lesson drawn from the parting. Though the young are brought forth in sorrow, after their dams have suckled them awhile they shift for themselves in the fields and are no more burdensome to them — which he makes an example to children, that when they have grown up they should not be always hanging upon their parents and craving from them, but put forth themselves to get their own livelihood and requite the care they received. The witnesses do not finally divide; whether corn or open country feeds them, all read the verse as the last stroke of a portrait in which God alone rears the wild things from the secret birth to the free and self-sufficient life, and does it without a herdsman's hand.
5:
The gallery moves from the mountain crags to the open desert, and the divine question turns from the wild goat's birth to the wild ass's liberty: "Who hath sent out the wild ass free?" The reformed John Gill hears the whole weight of the riddle in that word "free." The creature ranges the wide waste at pleasure, under no man's restraint; naturally wild, it is naturally averse to servitude, desirous of liberty, and maintains its liberty — not that it cannot be tamed, for Pliny speaks of some that were, but that it chooses freedom and, agreeable to its nature, is sent out free. And the question presses home: who gave this creature such a nature and such a longing after liberty, and the power and the cunning to keep clear of bondage? It is of God.

The wesleyan-arminian voices supply the zoology and the point. Adam Clarke identifies the pere with the onos agrios of the Greeks and the onager of the Latins, not to be confounded with the zebra; it is of a grey colour and so swift that no horse but the Arab barbs can overtake it, and it is found across Libya, Numidia, Syria, Persia, and Tartary, differing from the tame ass only in its independence and in being stronger and nimbler. He notes that the parallel term, arod, means the "brayer," so named from its frequent peculiar cry, and that it may be the same animal under another name — though Mr. Good supposes a distinct species, the jichta. John Wesley reduces the two clauses to their nerve: "sent," who gave him this disposition that he loves freedom and hates the subjection other creatures quietly endure; "loosed," who keeps him from receiving the bands and submitting to the service of man.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment carries across the wild ass, weighs the liberty and finds it a doubtful prize. Who but God has sent out the wild ass free? He has given a disposition to it, and therefore a dispensation for it; freedom from service and liberty to range at pleasure are but the privileges of a wild ass, and it is a pity that any of the children of men should covet such a liberty or value themselves upon it. It is better, Henry says, to labour and be good for something than to ramble and be good for nothing. The witnesses do not divide; they read the verse as God's claim to be the author of a wildness no man conferred, and as a quiet rebuke to Job, who could no more sign the wild ass's charter of freedom than he could recall it to the yoke.
6:
Having named the wild ass's freedom, the speech grants him a dwelling to match it, and the witnesses linger over the desolate estate God assigns his creature. The reformed John Gill reads "whose house I have made the wilderness" of a lodging fitted to the creature's nature — set at a distance from men, where he is in least danger of being brought into subjection; such were the deserts of Arabia, where Xenophon reports many of these swift creatures ranged, and where Leo Africanus found great numbers on the borders of the waste. The wilderness is not the wild ass's exile but his appointed mansion.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet — "Whose house I have made the wilderness, and the barren land his dwellings" — and pause, as is their manner, over the pointing of the Hebrew, noting the dagesh in the word for the wild ox that will follow and the retreat of the accent, small textual niceties that keep their eye on the exact letter even here. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke fixes the second term with a lexicographer's precision: "the barren land" is melechah, the salt land, or salt places, as the margin has it — a soil whose very sterility is the wild ass's freehold. It is a striking turn in the speech that God should call himself the maker of so desolate a homestead, appointing the salt waste as deliberately as he appointed the crags to the wild goat, so that even the wilderness is not lawless ground but a dwelling assigned.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry turns the unenclosed lodging into a parable of liberty and its cost. God has given the wild ass an unfenced house, the wilderness, where he has room enough to traverse his ways and to snuff up the wind at his pleasure, as the same creature is pictured doing in Jer. 2:24, as if he lived upon the air; for it is the barren land that is his dwelling. But observe the exchange, Henry says: the tame ass that labours and is serviceable to man has his master's crib to go to for both shelter and food, and lives in a fruitful land, while the wild ass that will have his liberty must take it in a barren land — "he that will not labour, let him not eat." The witnesses do not divide; whether the ground be called wilderness or salt-flat, all read the verse as God's deed of gift to his wild tenant, and as a reminder that the very independence Job's friends and Job himself might envy is housed, by God's own arrangement, in a country where nothing grows.
7:
The picture of the free creature sharpens into scorn, and the witnesses gather around the wild ass's contempt of the town and the taskmaster. The reformed John Gill reads "he scorneth the multitude of the city" of a creature that would rather be alone and free in the wilderness than a slave among a throng of men, like the tame ass; it despises and defies the crowd that might come out to take it. Gill piles up the ancient testimony to its speed — Leo Africanus says it yields to none for swiftness but the Barbary horse; Xenophon, that it exceeds the horse, outruns its pursuers, then stands and rests until they draw near before starting again, so that there is no taking it unless many hands are employed. He allows too that the clause may be rendered "the noise of the city," the stir and bustle it flees.

The wesleyan-arminian voices keep the same note. Adam Clarke says simply that the creature is so swift it cannot be run down, referring back to the description of its speed; John Wesley glosses that it scorns its pursuers, fearing them not because it is swift and can easily escape, and that as for "the driver," it will not be brought to receive his yoke nor do his drudgery. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the second clause with a philologist's ear: "the crying of the driver" is rather "the shoutings of the taskmaster," the word being the very one applied to the taskmasters of Egypt — which raises, he suggests, the question whether there may be here a reminiscence of that bondage, the free desert creature set against the enslaved brickmakers of the Nile.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the verse into his portrait of masterless liberty. Having no owner, the wild ass is in no subjection; if men attempt to take him and surround him with a multitude, he will soon get clear of them, and the crying of the driver is nothing to him. He laughs, as Bishop Patrick renders it, at those who live in the tumult and bustle of cities, thinking himself the happier in the wilderness — for opinion, Henry adds drily, is the rate of things. The witnesses do not divide; whether they hear in "the driver" a mere herdsman or, with Ellicott, an echo of Pharaoh's taskmasters, all read the verse as the wild ass's defiance of the harness and the crowd alike, another creature God made free of the very yoke Job could never lay upon it.
8:
The wild-ass panel closes on the creature's spare and roving pasture, and the witnesses read the poverty of the desert table as the price and proof of its freedom. The reformed John Gill glosses "the range of the mountains is his pasture" of a creature that ranges the hills for food, looking about — for the word, he notes, signifies to search — trying first one place and then another to get a little, for it keeps short commons there. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the same line within their strophe — "the range of the mountains is his pasture, and he searcheth after every green thing" — catching the restless quest across the barren heights. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke agrees that the mountains and desert places are the wild ass's peculiar pasture, where he lives on anything green, any vegetable production the waste affords; and John Wesley draws out the creature's own reckoning: he prefers that mean provision with his freedom before the fattest pastures with servitude.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the whole in the frame of providence and of Job's ignorance. Having no owner, the wild ass has no feeder, and no provision is made for him; he must shift for himself. The range of the mountains is his pasture, and a bare pasture it is, where he searches after here and there a green thing as he can find and pick it up, whereas the labouring asses have green things in plenty without their searching. And from the untameableness of this and the other creatures, Henry says, we may infer how unfit we are to give law to Providence, who cannot give law even to a wild ass's colt.

So the witnesses converge on the argument the divine speech is quietly building. The wild ass is not a creature abandoned but a creature provided for in a manner Job never devised — fed on the sparse green of the crags by a God who asks no leave of man. Wesley's proverb weighs the bargain from the beast's side: the mean fare of liberty is chosen over the full crib of the yoke. Gill and Keil and Delitzsch trace the daily searching, and Henry lifts the whole into its lesson, that the God who feeds and frees this one wild colt of the desert is beyond the reach of the man who had thought to reason with him and to set the world in better order. The panel ends, as it began, with a creature wholly outside Job's dominion and wholly inside God's care.
9:
The speech turns from creatures that merely flee man to one that flatly refuses his harness, and the question — "Will the unicorn be willing to serve thee, or abide by thy crib?" — opens the sharpest dispute of the chapter, for the witnesses cannot agree what beast the Hebrew reem names. The reformed John Gill treats the very existence of the fabled one-horned creature as an open question, the accounts of it being for the most part fabulous; though Vartomannus claimed to have seen two at Mecca out of Ethiopia, the larger with a horn three cubits long. There are indeed several "monocerots" — the rhinoceros, certain Indian asses, even the Greenland whale — but none of them answers the creature of Scripture, which must have been well known to Job and to Israel, and strong.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke is blunt: the "fine elegant animal like a horse, with one long curled horn," commonly called the unicorn, must be given up as fabulous, left to the heralds and their armorial bearings; it is no honour to the royal arms of Great Britain that so unreal a beast should be a supporter. The reem, he declares, is undoubtedly the rhinoceros, named from the horn on his nose and still called reem in Arabia; a savage creature whose hide, like armour, resists sabres, javelins, and even musket-balls, and whose untameable nature the following clauses are meant to display. Against this the grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott protests that it is a mistake to identify the animal with the rhinoceros, as was formerly done; it is more probably the buffalo or wild ox. The most glaring form of the error, he says, appears in Ps. 22:21, "the horns of the unicorns"; and the way the creature is here set in analogous contrast to the domestic ox, put to the same familiar and homely toil, suggests it is not wholly dissimilar to tame cattle. Keil and Delitzsch, the other grammatical-historical voice, render the word "oryx" and pose the question in kind: "Will the oryx be willing to serve thee, or will he lodge in thy crib?"

The other wesleyan-arminian witness, John Wesley, simply records the standoff — it is disputed whether this be the rhinoceros or a kind of wild bull — and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry leans to the latter, taking the reem for a strong, stately, proud creature, mighty as in Num. 23:22, able to serve but not willing, whom God challenges Job to force to the crib. So the debate is real and unresolved: rhinoceros, says Clarke; buffalo or wild ox, say Ellicott, Keil and Delitzsch, and Henry; while Gill and Wesley leave the name in doubt. What none of them doubts is the point of the question — that here is a strength Job cannot bend, a creature that will neither serve his turn nor stand at his manger.
10:
The challenge grows concrete and almost comic as God pictures Job trying to break the wild ox to the plough: "Canst thou bind the unicorn with his band in the furrow?" The reformed John Gill spells out the impossible scene — to put the yoke and harness upon him and fasten him to the plough, that he might draw it and cut furrows in the field, or break up the ground as the tame ox does. The answer is flat: thou canst not. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet with the same creature they name the oryx — "Canst thou bind the oryx in the furrow with a leading rein, or will he harrow the valleys, following thee?" — and set it in the strophe that runs on to the harvest, where the whole comedy of a wild beast pressed into farm-service is laid out for Job to weigh.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment carries across the unicorn's whole panel, presses the theology hidden in the picture. Thou canst not tame him, nor bind him with his band, nor set him to draw the harrow; for there are creatures willing to serve man, that seem to take a pleasure in serving him and to have a love for their masters, and there are others that will never be brought to serve him at all. And this refusal, Henry says, is itself an effect of sin. Man has revolted from his subjection to his Maker, and is therefore justly punished with the revolt of the inferior creatures from their subjection to him — yet, as a token of God's good-will, some are still serviceable, the tame bullock bending to the furrow where the wild ox never will.

So the witnesses read the verse as more than a lesson in husbandry. The image of the untamed strength that will not take the leading rein nor walk the valleys behind the ploughman is, in the movement of the divine speech, another sounding of Job's littleness: he cannot so much as harness one wild beast to his field, much less order the world he had presumed to arraign. Gill fixes the plain sense of the yoke and the furrow; Keil and Delitzsch keep the exact wording of the band and the harrowed valleys; Henry lifts the whole into the doctrine of a creation that mirrors, in its half-broken obedience, both man's fall from his Maker and the mercy that still leaves him some willing servants. The reem stands in the furrow God set before Job, and will not move at his word — a strength that answers to a higher hand than his.
11:
The question of harnessing the wild ox sharpens into a question of trust, God asking whether Job would dare rely on so great a strength: "Wilt thou trust him, because his strength is great?" The reformed John Gill draws the contrast with the tame ox, which is employed precisely because it is strong to labour and, being manageable, may be trusted to plough or tread out the corn under direction. The wild ox, though stronger still and so the fitter for labour, is yet not to be trusted, being unruly and unmanageable. Gill weighs whether the creature meant might be the uri of which Caesar wrote, and finds the description apt: those wild oxen, a little smaller than elephants, of the kind and colour and shape of a bull, were of great strength and great swiftness, and not to be tamed — strength enough for any work, and no submission to put it to use.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse to the same effect within their strophe — "Wilt thou trust him because his strength is great, and leave thy labour to him?" — setting the beast's raw power against the confidence it can never earn. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the point into its lesson: thou darest not trust him; though his strength is great, thou wilt not leave thy labour to him as thou dost with the asses or oxen that a little child may lead or drive, leaving to them all the pains. For a disposition to labour, Henry says, is as much the gift of God as an ability for it; and it is a great mercy if, where God gives strength for service, he gives a heart to serve — a thing we should pray for and reason ourselves into, which the brute creatures cannot do.

So the witnesses make the verse a meditation on strength without submission. The reem has power in abundance and no will to bend it to man's use, and this, in the argument God is unfolding, is the very reason Job cannot command him: not weakness in the beast but a wildness of nature that no strength can supply. Gill's account of Caesar's untameable oxen, Keil and Delitzsch's careful rendering of the trust that cannot be reposed, and Henry's doctrine that the heart to labour is God's separate gift all converge on one confession — that the mightiest creature is useless to Job unless a willing spirit answer to its might, and that such willingness lies, like the strength itself, in the giving hand of God alone.
12:
God carries the picture through to the harvest, asking whether the wild ox could ever be relied on to bring the crop home: "Wilt thou believe him, that he will bring home thy seed, and gather it into thy barn?" The reformed John Gill lets the plain sense answer itself — wilt thou believe he will draw in the cart and bring home the ripe sheaves as the tame ox does? No; thou knowest him too well to believe he will bring it home in safety. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reduces it to a sentence: thou canst make no domestic nor agricultural use of him at all. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott sharpens the verb, noting that "wilt thou believe him" means "wilt thou trust him," or better "wilt thou feel confidence in him," matching the "trust" of the verse before; and Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet in the same key — "Wilt thou confide in him to bring in thy sowing, and to garner thy threshing-floor?" — closing the strophe on the barn door the wild beast will never darken.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the harvest image into the moral of the whole panel. Because the wild ox will not serve about the corn, Henry observes, he is not so well fed as the tame ox, whose mouth was not to be muzzled in treading out the corn; the willing servant shares the grain, the wild refuser does not. And the reason lies deeper than appetite: he that made the creature never designed him for the plough or the cart, and a beast that has no mind to take pains or to do good may justly be reckoned wild and abandoned, as, among men, may those who likewise will neither labour nor be of use.

So the witnesses close the unicorn's panel where it began, on the gap between strength and service. The reem could carry any load and gather any harvest, but Job could never trust him to do it, for the will is wanting; and this, in the divine speech, is one more proof of how narrow Job's dominion really is. He cannot so much as count on a wild beast to fetch his own grain to his own barn. Gill and Clarke fix the useless might, Ellicott and Keil and Delitzsch weigh the confidence that cannot be placed, and Henry draws the lesson that runs through all — that the creature serves, or refuses, according to the disposition its Maker gave or withheld, and that the ordering even of the harvest lies in a wisdom and a will not Job's own.
13:
The gallery passes from beasts to birds, and at once the witnesses fall into a dispute over the very name of the creature, for the question — "Gavest thou the goodly wings unto the peacocks?" — may not concern the peacock at all. The reformed John Gill reads "ostriches" with the Vulgate and the Tigurine version, and takes Montanus's "the wing of those that exult is joyful" of the ostrich, who in the confidence of her wings exults over the horse and his rider. The peacock, he objects, is remarkable not for its wings but for its tail, whereas the ostrich's wings are as sails, so that with them she runs or rows rather than flies — whence Plautus called her the "sea sparrow." Besides, Gill doubts the peacock was even known in Job's country and time, being a bird of the Indies, brought to Judea only under Solomon and unknown in Greece and Rome until later ages.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke presses the philology further, and would unsettle nearly every name in the line. Peacocks are not intended; renanim should be rendered "ostriches"; chasidah, which the Authorized Version gives as "ostrich," should be "stork," as it is elsewhere; and notsah, translated "feathers," may be "hawk" or "pelican." He cites the Vulgate — "the feather of the ostrich is like to that of the stork and the hawk" — and Mr. Good's neat resolution: "the wing of the ostrich tribe is for flapping, but of the stork and falcon for flight." The ostrich's wings cannot raise her, but by their perpetual vibration, catching the wind, they give her a rapidity of running beyond any other animal — Adanson's tame ostriches, he reports, would have distanced the fleetest English racehorses. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott renders the whole as a contrast — "the wing of the ostrich is superb, but are her pinions and feathers like the stork's?" — noting that ostrich feathers, worth eight to fifteen pounds a pound weight, are beautiful and valuable but scarcely a bird's true plumage, useless for flight, while the bird itself runs like a quadruped at fifty or sixty miles an hour. Keil and Delitzsch render in the same vein: "the wing of the ostrich vibrates joyously; is she pious, wing and feather?"

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry alone keeps the peacock in view alongside the ostrich, reading the verse of something the two birds have in common — beautiful feathers, for fine feathers make proud birds, and the peacock is an emblem of pride whom Solomon in all his glory did not outshine. Yet the ostrich too has goodly feathers and is a foolish bird, so that wisdom does not always go with beauty; who, Henry asks, would not rather have the voice of the nightingale than the tail of the peacock? So the debate stands drawn: the bird is the ostrich, not the peacock, say Gill, Clarke, Ellicott, and Keil and Delitzsch, with Clarke and Ellicott further making chasidah the stork; while Henry holds both birds in the frame at once. The divine speech has left the witnesses arguing over renderings and names, which is precisely the ground on which these verses are fought.
14:
The ostrich's folly begins with her nest, and the witnesses read the abandoned eggs as the first mark of a strange and careless bird. The reformed John Gill takes "which leaveth her eggs in the earth" quite literally: she lays them and leaves them. Aelianus, he notes, describes her building a low nest in the ground, scooping a hollow in the sand with her feet, though mistaken as to the number of eggs; Leo Africanus more truly reckons ten or twelve, each the size of a cannon-ball and weighing some fifteen pounds. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet plainly — "which leaveth her eggs in the earth, and warmeth them in dust" — the mother's whole care committed to the sand.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the travellers' testimony to this want of parental affection, which he says is almost universally acknowledged. Mr. Jackson, in his account of Morocco, reports that the ostrich, having laid her eggs, goes away, forgetting or forsaking them, so that if another ostrich finds them she hatches them as if they were her own, so deficient is the bird's recollection. And from Dr. Shaw's fuller account Clarke draws the picture of a hen that lays from thirty to fifty eggs, sets the first in the centre and ranges the rest about it, thrusts them into the earth and warms them in the sand, reserving the greater part not for a brood at all but for food to feed the young she does hatch. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott adds the one touch of method in the madness: the ostrich sits upon her eggs only at night, when the cold would chill and destroy them, while by day the heat of the sand carries on the hatching.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, whose comment runs across the ostrich's whole portrait, sets the carelessness against the instinct of other birds. She does not retire to some private place and make a nest, as the sparrow and swallow do in Ps. 84:3, and there lay and hatch; most creatures are strangely guided by natural instinct to preserve their young, but the ostrich is a monster in nature, dropping her eggs anywhere upon the ground and taking no care to hatch them. If the sand and the sun will hatch them, well and good, for she will not warm them. The witnesses do not divide; whether they count the eggs with Gill, weigh the sand's warmth with Ellicott, or marvel at the desertion with Clarke and Henry, all read the verse as the divine speech setting the ostrich's improvidence, deliberately, against the tender care that carried the wild goats' births safely through — one wisdom given, another withheld, and both alike God's doing.
15:
The carelessness deepens into a positive hazard, for the eggs left in the open lie under every passing foot: she "forgetteth that the foot may crush them, and that the wild beast may break them." The reformed John Gill draws the danger out concretely — the foot of the traveller may crush them, laid as they are in the ground where he walks, or on the sand of the seashore where he may tread and trample them unawares to pieces; and to prevent all this, he says, the creature has no foresight at all. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse in the same double stroke: she forgets "that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may break them," the eggs exposed alike to man and to the ranging beast.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the traveller's report confirming the sacred text to the letter. The very account of the forsaken eggs, he says, illustrates this word — that she "forgetteth that the foot may crush them, or that the wild beast may break them" — and he marvels how exactly the poet is acquainted with every part of his subject, so that incontestable facts confirm all he says. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry presses the question the verse cannot help raising: if she takes no care to preserve them, and the foot of the traveller may crush them and the wild beast break them, how then are any young ones brought forth, and whence is it that the species has not perished from the earth?

Henry offers the two answers the case allows, and they are answers about providence, not about the bird. We must suppose, he says, either that God, by a special providence, with the heat of the sun and the sand hatches the neglected eggs of the ostrich, as he feeds the neglected young ones of the raven, or else that, though the ostrich often leaves her eggs thus, she does not always. Either way the survival of the creature is thrown back upon the God who watches what the mother forgets. So the witnesses converge: Gill on the bird's utter want of foresight, Keil and Delitzsch on the twofold peril of foot and beast, Clarke on the travellers' confirmation, and Henry on the providence that alone keeps a heedless species alive. The divine speech dwells on the ostrich's improvidence not to mock the bird but to press upon Job how much of the world's continuance hangs, unseen, upon a care that is wholly God's, exercised over creatures that do nothing to secure themselves.
16:
The verse names the ostrich's fault outright — she is "hardened against her young ones, as though they were not hers" — and the witnesses weigh both the harshness and a puzzle in it. The reformed John Gill, unwilling to let the charge fall without qualification, cites Aelianus that the ostrich is in fact very tender of the young she hatches, even exposing herself to danger for them. The hardness, he suggests, lies rather in her forgetfulness: having laid her eggs in the sand she forgets where, and finding other eggs sits and hatches them and regards those as her own, so that she is hardened against her true and real young as though they did not belong to her. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke keeps the plainer and grimmer picture, drawn from Dr. Shaw: she neglects her little ones, which are often found half-starved, straggling and moaning about like so many deserted orphans, seeking a mother that does not return.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the whole and attend to its grammar — "she treateth her young ones harshly, as if they were not hers; in vain is her labour, without her being distressed" — noting that the verb "hardened" stands, oddly, in the masculine though used of the hen-ostrich, a liberty the Hebrew allows, and that Jerome caught the sense with quasi non sint sui, "as though they were not her own." By the harshness of her conduct, they explain, she treats her young as strangers to her, and her labour of laying and brooding comes to nothing, yet without any anxiety on her part.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gives the moral its edge. To be hardened against any is unlovely even in a brute creature, much more against one's own young ones, which cannot help themselves and therefore merit compassion, and which, being parts of herself, she treats as though they were not hers. Her labour in laying her eggs is in vain and all lost, Henry says, because she has not that fear and tender concern for them she should have; and he turns it to a proverb — those are most likely to lose their labour who are least in fear of losing it. So the witnesses circle a single wonder without wholly agreeing on its shape: Gill and Aelianus would soften the cruelty into mere forgetfulness, hardening the bird only against the young she has muddled and lost; Clarke, Henry, and Keil and Delitzsch let the plainer charge stand, that she is callous toward her own. Either way the divine speech makes the ostrich's want of natural affection a marvel set deliberately beside the wild goat's careful nurture — the same God who put tenderness in the one withheld it from the other, and neither can Job explain.
17:
The reason for the ostrich's folly is at last laid bare, and it is a reason that reaches back to God himself: "because God hath deprived her of wisdom, neither hath he imparted to her understanding." The reformed John Gill notes that the verb may be rendered "made her to forget" the wisdom she had, and points to her proverbial short memory — Leo Africanus reports the bird presently forgets the very place where its eggs are laid. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet flatly to the same sense, that Eloah has caused her to forget wisdom and given her no share of understanding, so that the bird's stupidity is traced not to accident but to a withholding hand.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke heaps up the ancients' testimony to that stupidity. She covers her head in the reeds, he says, and thinks herself wholly hidden because she cannot see, as Claudian describes; hunters draw the skin of an ostrich's neck over one hand as a lure sufficient to take her with the other; and she has so little brain that Heliogabalus, it is said, had six hundred heads served for a single supper. Clarke pauses, with Dr. Young, to admire how the sacred author just touches the great point of distinction in each creature and then hastens on — for a likeness is lost in too much description, and a meaning in too much illustration. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley states the theology of the withholding without adornment: God has not implanted in her that instinct and affection which he has put into other birds and beasts toward their young.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws out the lesson the verse presses. This intimates, he says, that the art which other animals have to nourish and preserve their young is God's gift, and that where it does not exist God has denied it — so that by the folly of the ostrich, as well as by the wisdom of the ant, we may learn to be wise. The witnesses do not divide. Whether they call it a wisdom forgotten, as Gill, or a wisdom never given, as Wesley and Keil and Delitzsch, all read the verse as the plainest word in the whole gallery about the sovereignty of the Giver: the same God who lavished cunning on the hawk and love on the stork simply withheld both from the ostrich, and the bird's very defects are as much his handiwork as the eagle's excellences. The divine speech will let Job draw the inference — that if God so freely apportions wisdom and folly among the birds, the ordering of Job's own darkened lot is no less his to dispose.
18:
For all her folly the ostrich has one glory, and the verse springs it as a surprise: the moment she rouses herself, "she scorneth the horse and his rider." The reformed John Gill notes that the bird, sometimes eight feet high, raises herself from the ground when alarmed and erects her wings for flight, or rather for running. The wesleyan-arminian voices dwell on the speed. Adam Clarke explains that she neither flies nor runs distinctly, but has a motion composed of both, using her wings as sails to make great speed; Xenophon, he adds, said Cyrus had horses that could overtake the goat and the wild ass, but none that could reach this creature, and a horse that could equal her was priced at a thousand golden ducats or a hundred camels. John Wesley reads the scorn of the same swiftness: she lifts up her head and body and spreads her wings, and despises her pursuers, for though she cannot fly, by the aid of her wings she runs so fast that horsemen cannot reach her.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott, however, turns the verse in a direction the others do not follow. He takes "she lifteth up herself" of the bird rising either from the nest at maturity or as she sets out to run, and notes that the ostrich runs in a curve, which alone allows horsemen to overtake and take her. But then, recalling that the earlier verse seemed to draw a comparison between the ostrich and the stork, Ellicott suggests that here too, probably, the subject is the stork: for swift and powerful as the ostrich is, no sooner does the stork, on the contrary, rise on high into the air than she, like any bird, can baffle the pursuit of horsemen altogether. It is a reading peculiar to him, shifting the scorn from the running ostrich to the soaring stork.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry keeps to the ostrich and finds in her flight the sharp irony of the whole portrait. She leaves her eggs in danger, but if she herself be in danger, no creature strives more to get out of the way; then she lifts up her wings on high — the strength of them now standing her in better stead than their beauty — and runs so fast that a horseman at full speed cannot overtake her, so that she scorns the horse and his rider. Those least under the law of natural affection, Henry observes, often contend most for the law of self-preservation. So the witnesses close the ostrich's panel with her one triumph, agreeing that the careless mother is a matchless runner, and differing only in Ellicott's solitary turn toward the stork; and the verse, with its scornful horse and rider, hands the speech neatly on to the war-horse that comes next.
19:
The gallery reaches its most splendid figure, and the question itself has the ring of a fanfare: "Hast thou given the horse strength? hast thou clothed his neck with thunder?" The reformed John Gill observes that it is the war-horse throughout that is meant, and that his strength denotes not bodily force only but fortitude and courage, both alike the gift of God and not of man. The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sets the horse against the wild creatures just described: God, having shown his power in beasts that are strong and despise man, now shows it in one scarcely inferior in strength yet tame and serviceable, whose neck is clothed with thunder in a large and flowing mane that makes him formidable. He uses his strength for man but has it from God, who nevertheless delights not in the strength of the horse, as Ps. 147:10 says, and has told us that a horse is a vain thing for safety in Ps. 33:17.

The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke devotes his longest note in the chapter to this description, recording the famous critique from the Guardian that set the sacred poet beside Homer and Virgil and found the classical descriptions faint by comparison; for while the heathen poets paint the outward figure and motions of the horse, the sacred writer makes all the beauties flow from an inward principle in the creature. On the phrase "clothed his neck with thunder," Clarke weighs the bold figure: Homer and Virgil mention only the mane, but the metaphor of thunder expresses at once the shaking of that flowing hair, whose flakes suggest the idea of lightning, and the violent force and agitation of the neck. The original word, he says, Bochart and other learned men take of the floating mane, from a verb meaning to toss or agitate, and Clarke declares himself satisfied that the tossing mane is here meant.

The grammatical-historical witnesses read the thunder otherwise. Charles Ellicott glosses it "with terror, such as thunder causes," though he allows that some refer it to the moving or shaking of the mane; John Wesley calls it simply "a strong metaphor, to denote force and terror"; and Keil and Delitzsch render the line "dost thou clothe his neck with flowing hair," coming down, like Clarke, on the mane. So a genuine difference plays over the image: whether the horse's neck is clothed with the terror that thunder inspires, as Ellicott and Wesley hear it, or with the storm of the tossing mane, as Clarke and Keil and Delitzsch prefer. The witnesses do not divide over the grandeur, only over its figure; and all agree with Gill's first word, that the strength and the courage alike were poured into the creature by God, so that the question strips Job of any share in the making of the noblest servant he owns.
20:
The divine speech dwells on the horse's terrible vigour, though the very words are disputed: "Canst thou make him afraid as a grasshopper? the glory of his nostrils is terrible." The reformed John Gill offers two ways to take the first clause — either, canst thou make him timid and easily frightened as a grasshopper, which the horse is not; or rather, canst thou make him skip and leap like a grasshopper, giving him that faculty of leaping hedges and ditches for which the horse is famous, as Neptune's war-horses were said to be good leapers. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch decide firmly for the leaping: the motion intended, they say, is fixed by the comparison with the grasshopper — a curved bounding forward in leaps, now to the right, now to the left, the very caracol of the riding-schools; and the "snorting," they add, is not the neighing but the sound blown through the nostrils, whose terror the verse celebrates.

The other grammatical-historical voice, Charles Ellicott, renders the clause outright "Hast thou made him to leap as a locust?", refusing the older "make him afraid" altogether. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke reports yet a third reading, from Mr. Good, "Hast thou given him to launch forth as an arrow?" — arguing that the word commonly rendered "grasshopper" may mean an arrow, and that the verb, signifying to tremble, quiver, rush, and dart forth, unites the two ideas of rapidity and flashing motion. So the verse carries a real division of renderings: "make him afraid," as the received text and Gill's first sense have it; "make him leap like a locust," as Keil and Delitzsch and Ellicott prefer; or "launch him forth like an arrow," as Clarke by Good would read.

Over the second clause the witnesses are of one mind, and the puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry voices it: the horse's neck and nostrils look great, and the glory of his nostrils, when he snorts and flings up his head and throws the foam about, is terrible. Henry supposes there may have been at that time and in that country a statelier breed of horses than any now known, to answer so lofty a description. The witnesses do not divide over the majesty of the snorting beast; they part only over the trembling or the bounding of the first line, and the divine speech leaves the exact word an open question while the picture — a creature whose very breath is dreadful — stands unmistakable. Whatever the verb, the point holds against Job: he neither made the horse's courage nor can he counterfeit its terror.
21:
The speech sets the war-horse in motion, pawing the ground in his eagerness for the charge: "He paweth in the valley, and rejoiceth in his strength: he goeth on to meet the armed men." The reformed John Gill places him where armies pitch, in the valley convenient for cavalry, impatient of standing still, rising on his fore-feet and pawing and prancing, digging at the earth with a continual striking. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley confirms the ground, noting that battles, and especially horse-battles, were commonly pitched in the valleys or low grounds. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke seizes on the verb, rendering "they dig in the valley," for in the violence of his galloping the horse scoops up sods out of the earth at every pitch of his body — the very image, he notes, that Virgil caught in his cavat tellurem, "he scoops out the ground."

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott attends to a nicety the others pass over: the first verb is plural and the second singular, so that the line reads, strictly, "they paw" — literally, they dig — "and he rejoiceth," a small shift of number within the sentence. Keil and Delitzsch render the whole in their heroic key: "he paweth the ground in the plain, and boundeth about with strength; he advanceth to meet an armed host." The picture is of a creature so charged with vigour that it cannot keep its footing still, but tears at the valley floor while it waits to be loosed upon the enemy.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the horse's spirit as a kind of noble pride, and draws it into contrast with the wild ass. See how frolicsome he is, Henry says: he paws in the valley, scarcely knowing what ground he stands upon, proud of his strength — and with far more reason to be so than the wild ass of v.8, for he uses his strength in the service of man and under his direction, while the wild ass used his only in contempt of man and in revolt from him. And see how forward he is to engage, going on to meet the armed men, eager for the very danger. The witnesses do not divide; whether they read "he paweth" or "they dig," all see in the restless, prancing beast a courage poured into it by God, and the divine speech presses the contrast that the horse's spirited obedience, no less than the wild ass's masterless liberty, is a thing Job neither gave nor can command — a strength that answers gladly to the trumpet it was made to hear.
22:
The horse's courage rises to its boldest pitch as the speech turns to his contempt of danger: "He mocketh at fear, and is not affrighted; neither turneth he back from the sword." The reformed John Gill reads the mockery of all that strikes fear and fright into men — arms, though ever so terrible, and armies, though never so numerous; the war-horse makes light of what would appal his rider. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line to the same effect, that he laughs at fear and is not affrighted and turns not back from the sword, catching the sheer fearlessness the verse celebrates. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke preserves the old strength of Coverdale's version — "he layeth aside all feare, his stomach is not abated, neither starteth he aback for eny swerde" — the courage undiminished before the naked blade.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the fearlessness into a portrait and then into a warning. See how fearless the horse is, Henry says: he despises death and the most threatening dangers, mocks at fear and makes a jest of it; slash at him with a sword, rattle the quiver, brandish the spear to drive him back, and he will not retreat but presses forward, and even inspires courage into his rider. And this description, Henry adds, helps to explain the character given of presumptuous sinners in Jer. 8:6, "every one turneth to his course, as the horse rusheth into the battle." When a man's heart is fully set in him to do evil, and he is carried on in a wicked way by the violence of his appetites and passions, there is no making him afraid of the wrath of God or the fatal consequences of sin; let conscience set the curse of the law and all the terrors of the Almighty in battle-array before him, he mocks at this fear and is not affrighted, nor turns back from the flaming sword.

So the witnesses read the verse on two levels at once. On the surface it is the plainest praise of the war-horse, whose valour before the sword is a wonder of the creature's inward make; and beneath it Henry hears a caution, that the same undauntedness which is a glory in the beast is a peril in the man who has hardened himself against God. The voices do not divide over the sense of the line — Gill, Clarke, and Keil and Delitzsch agree with Henry on the horse's dauntless spirit; and the divine speech presses the wonder home to Job, that a courage he never instilled, and could not instil, was breathed into this creature by the God whose questions he is being made to answer. The horse fears nothing but the hand that made him bold.
23:
The arming of the enemy only feeds the horse's ardour, for the very clash of weapons about him leaves him unmoved: "The quiver rattleth against him, the glittering spear and the shield." The reformed John Gill weighs two ways of taking the rattling quiver. It may stand for the arrows that come whizzing about the horse from the enemy, which do not intimidate him; or it may be the quiver of arrows carried upon his own back, rattling as he runs, for Homer and Virgil, he notes, speak of the sounding quiver borne on the shoulder — though Gill judges the first sense the better, the missiles of the foe rattling harmlessly around a beast that will not flinch. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley takes the plainer of the two, that the quiver is here put for the arrows contained in it, which, shot against the horse and his rider, make a rattling noise as they come.

The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the verse "the quiver rattleth over him, the glittering lance and spear," setting the flash of the weapons against the horse's steadiness; and the wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gives both Mr. Good's version, "against him rattleth the quiver, the glittering spear and the shield," and Coverdale's older line, "though the qyvers rattle upon him, though the speare and shilde glistre," yet still, as the sequel runs, he rushes on. The whole armoury of battle is spread before the creature only to be despised.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry folds the verse into the horse's dauntless charge: rattle the quiver at him, brandish the spear and shield to turn him back, and he will not retreat, but presses forward into the very danger. The witnesses do not divide over the wonder, and part only, mildly, over the direction of the rattling — whether it is the enemy's arrows that whistle about him, as Gill on the whole prefers and Wesley reads, or the quiver borne upon his own galloping back. Either way the point of the divine speech holds: the din and glitter of arms that would scatter any timid creature, and unnerve the boldest man, cannot move this horse a step from his course. His steadiness under the rattling quiver and the flashing spear is one more mark of a courage God alone contrived, and Job least of all, who could no more make a beast defy the sword than he could himself outface the terrors he had wished to reason away.
24:
The horse's fury gathers to a headlong rush, so that he seems to devour the very earth beneath him: "He swalloweth the ground with fierceness and rage: neither believeth he that it is the sound of the trumpet." The reformed John Gill reads the first clause of the creature's prodigious swiftness: so eager for the battle, so full of fierceness and rage, he bounds over the plain so fast that he seems rather to swallow up the ground than to run upon it. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke, in the Guardian's critique, calls "he swalloweth the ground" an expression for prodigious swiftness in use among the Arabians, Job's countrymen, to this very day, and reckons it the boldest and noblest of all images for speed, matched only by the poets' pictures of a courser that leaves the plain crossed before he has fairly started.

Over the second clause the witnesses differ in tone. The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott reads "neither believeth he" of the horse disregarding the summons of the trumpet, as though he did not believe that it gave the call to war — a beast so battle-hungry he cannot credit that the awaited signal has come. The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley turns the same clause to gladness rather than disregard: the horse is so full of rage that he champs his bridle and is ready to tear and devour the very ground he stands on, and he is so pleased with the approach of battle and the sound of the trumpet calling to it that he can scarcely believe his ears for very joy. Keil and Delitzsch render the line "with fierceness and rage he swalloweth the ground, and standeth not still when the trumpet soundeth," making the point his utter refusal to be held back.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry sees the same furious violence, the horse curvetting and prancing and running with such heat against the enemy that one would think he swallowed the ground with fierceness and rage; and he remarks that high mettle is the praise of a horse rather than of a man, whom fierceness and rage ill become. So the witnesses agree entirely on the swallowed ground and the unbridled rush, and differ only in reading the horse's disbelief — whether, with Ellicott, he disregards the trumpet as if not believing the call has truly sounded, or, with Wesley, cannot believe his own ears for gladness that it has. Either way the divine speech has drawn a creature all fire and forward motion, whose eagerness for the fray Job neither kindled nor can restrain; and the very trumpet the horse strains to hear brings the panel to its climax in the verse that follows.
25:
The war-horse finds his voice, and the speech lets him answer the trumpet with a cry of his own: "He saith among the trumpets, Ha, ha; and he smelleth the battle afar off, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting." The reformed John Gill hears in that "ha, ha" the horse's pleasure in the sound of the trumpets, a rejoicing which he signifies by his neighing. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke finds the original peculiarly emphatical: the word is He'ach, a strong, partly nasal, partly guttural sound, exactly resembling the first note the horse emits in neighing, and the harsh gutturals of the following clause — "for from afar he scenteth the battle" — are wonderfully expressive of the creature's fierce anticipation; Coverdale's homely "Tush, sayeth he," Clarke thinks, catches the same disdainful eagerness.

The grammatical-historical Charles Ellicott glosses "among the trumpets" more exactly as "when there are plenty of trumpets," that is, as often as the trumpet soundeth, the horse answering every blast; and Keil and Delitzsch render the whole "he saith at every blast of the trumpet, Ha, ha! and from afar he scenteth the battle, the thundering of the captains and the shout of war." The wesleyan-arminian John Wesley reads the "ha, ha" as an expression of joy and alacrity uttered in his proud neighings, and takes the "thunder" of the last clause of the loud and joyful clamour begun by the commanders and taken up by the soldiers as they are ready to join battle.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry gathers the panel to its height. The sound of the trumpet, the thunder of the captains, and the shouting of the soldiers are, he says, as bellows to the fire of the horse's innate courage, making him spring forward with the utmost eagerness, as if he cried, "Ha, ha!"; and how wonderfully, Henry marvels, are the brute-creatures fitted for and inclined to the very services for which they were designed. The witnesses do not divide; whether they render the cry He'ach or "ha, ha" or "Tush," all hear in it the creature's joy in the very danger men dread, and read the scented battle and the answered trumpet as the crown of a courage wholly of God's making. The divine speech has brought its noblest servant to a pitch of glad ferocity Job could never have devised, and hands the argument on from the beasts of war to the birds of the air.
26:
The gallery lifts from the battlefield to the sky, and the question turns to the bird of passage whose migration no man taught her: "Doth the hawk fly by thy wisdom, and stretch her wings toward the south?" The reformed John Gill takes the flight of the hawk — swift, steady, and constant until she seizes her prey — and notes that the Vulgate and some others read instead "doth she grow feathered," of the bird's fledging, or of the yearly casting and renewing of her plumage; but whether her flight or her feathers be meant, neither is owing to men, but to the Lord who gives both. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke identifies the hawk, called nets from its swift darting upon the prey, with the falcon, and marvels at its speed — a strong falcon has flown from Westphalia to Prussia in a day, and one is said to have crossed from London to Paris in a night, so that the Egyptians made the bird the emblem of the wind. On "toward the south" he explains the migration: most of the falcon tribe pass the spring and summer in cold climates and wing their way to warmer regions at the approach of winter, and he asks whether it is through Job's teaching that any bird of passage knows the precise time to fly and the direction to take, citing the stork that knows her appointed times in Jer. 8:7.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry opens the bird-panel with the same wonder, that the fowls of the air are proofs of God's power and providence no less than the beasts of the earth. The hawk, a noble bird of strength and sagacity yet a bird of prey, is noticed for her flight, swift and strong, and especially for her southward course, following the sun in winter out of the colder countries of the north, particularly when she is to cast and renew her plumes; this is her wisdom, and it was God, not man, that gave it. It is a pity, Henry adds, that the reclaimed hawk, taught to fly at man's command for his sport, should ever be abused to the dishonour of the God from whom she has the wisdom that makes her flight serviceable.

The grammatical-historical witnesses attend to the flight and the structure of the speech. John Wesley glosses that the hawk flies so strongly, constantly, and swiftly, and stretches toward the south at winter's approach because she cannot bear the cold; and Charles Ellicott, standing back to survey the movement of the whole passage, remarks that a more symmetrical order would have set the ostrich after the war-horse and before the hawk, so that there might be a gradual transition from the fleetest of quadrupeds to the fleetest of birds by way of the ostrich, which, though winged like a bird, cannot use its wings as birds do but only runs upon the ground. The witnesses do not divide; whether the marvel be the hawk's fledging, as Gill's Vulgate would have it, or her unerring migration, as Clarke and Wesley read, all confess a wisdom in the bird that is God's gift and not Job's teaching — the sky itself governed by an instruction Job never gave.
27:
The speech mounts higher still, to the royal bird that soars beyond man's sight and sight of man: "Doth the eagle mount up at thy command, and make her nest on high?" The reformed John Gill answers the question with a flat no: not at Job's command, but by an instinct God has placed in her and a capacity he has given her above all other birds. Where other birds take a circuit and bend about before they soar, the eagle steers her course directly upward toward heaven, until she is out of sight and, as Apuleius says, up among the clouds. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet within their closing strophe — "or is it at thy command that the eagle soareth aloft, and buildeth its nest on high?" — setting the bird's lofty flight and loftier nest beyond the reach of any human bidding.

The wesleyan-arminian voices add the eagle's marvels. Adam Clarke notes that she is of so acute a sight that, when she is so high in the air that men cannot see her, she can yet discern a small fish in the water below; and John Wesley marks the height of the flight itself, that she mounts directly upward till she is out of sight, which no other bird can do. The point of the divine question, for all of them, is that this mounting is no achievement of Job's, who can neither command the ascent nor follow it with his eye.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry reads the eagle as a royal bird that is yet a bird of prey, the very permission and empowering of which, he says, may help to reconcile us to the prosperity of oppressors among men. She is noticed first for the height of her flight: no bird soars so high, has so strong a wing, nor can so well bear the light of the sun. "Doth she mount at thy command?" Henry has God ask; "is it by any strength she has from thee, or dost thou direct her flight? No; it is by the natural power and instinct God has given her that she will soar out of thy sight, much more out of thy call." The witnesses do not divide; all read the verse as the speech reaching its highest point, the desert floor left far below, and confessing that the eagle's mounting wing, like the hawk's migration and the horse's courage before it, is a gift of God that owes nothing to the man who is being made to see how small his command really is.
28:
From the height of her flight the speech turns to the height of her home, the eagle's nest set where no hand can reach it: "She dwelleth and abideth on the rock, upon the crag of the rock, and the strong place." The reformed John Gill reads it of a lodging where she and her young are safe: Pliny, he notes, says eagles make their nests in the rocks, even in the precipices of them, and here the bird is set upon the very tooth or edge of the rock, inaccessible, and so like a strongly fortified place. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke sharpens the Hebrew: "the crag of the rock" is shen sela, the tooth of the rock, some projecting point whither adventurous man himself dares not follow her; and "the strong place," metsudah, Mr. Good would render "ravine" and join to the verse that follows. The grammatical-historical Keil and Delitzsch render the line "it inhabiteth the rock, and buildeth its nest upon the crag of the rock and fastness," gathering all the words of height and strength into one picture of an unassailable eyrie.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry makes the eagle's stronghold a parable of false security. Her house, he says, is her castle and her stronghold; she makes it on high and on the rock, the crag of the rock, which sets her and her young out of the reach of danger. And so secure sinners think themselves as safe in their sins as the eagle in her nest on high, in the clefts of the rock; but "I will bring thee down thence, saith the LORD," in the word spoken against Edom's eagle-nest in Jer. 49:16. The higher bad men sit above the resentments of the earth, Henry warns, the nearer they ought to think themselves to the vengeance of heaven.

So the witnesses read the verse both as natural history and as a sounding of Job's reach. Gill, Clarke, and Keil and Delitzsch fix the sheer inaccessibility of the eyrie, the tooth of the rock where man dares not climb; Henry lifts the picture into its moral, that the loftiest security is no security against God. The divine speech, which has just shown Job an eagle he cannot command to mount, now shows him an eagle he cannot follow to her rest; and the crag of the rock, safe from every human assault, is safe only because the God who set the bird there keeps the one hand that can reach it. The verse leaves Job at the foot of a fastness he can neither scale nor shake — and prepares the eagle's quick eye and bloody table that the last verses will unfold.
29:
From her fortress on the crag the eagle turns her eye upon the world below, and the speech marks the far-seeing gaze that finds her food: "From thence she seeketh the prey, and her eyes behold afar off." The reformed John Gill pictures her upon the high rock, whence she looks down into the valleys and even into the sea, and spies whatever serves her purpose — lambs, fawns, geese, shellfish — though they lie in the most hidden and secret places; and he notes that the original says, more strongly, that she "diggeth" the prey, as men dig and diligently search for treasure hidden in secret, so keen is the sight for which she is fitted. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke gathers the ancients' proverbs for that sight, the eagle being famed for a strong and clear eye: Horace, Aelian, and Homer all bear witness, the last calling her the most quick-sighted of all fowls under heaven. John Wesley, the other wesleyan-arminian voice, marvels that her sight is so sharp and strong that she can look upon the sun with open eyes and yet behold the smallest prey upon the earth or the sea when she is mounted out of our sight.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry, having praised the eagle's mounting wing, notices now that her eyes behold afar off — not upward, but downward, in quest of her prey; and here he turns the bird into an emblem of the hypocrite. In this, Henry says, she is like a man who, while in the profession of religion he seems to rise toward heaven, keeps his eye and his heart upon the prey on earth, some temporal advantage, some widow's house or other that he hopes to devour under pretence of devotion. It is a reading peculiar to Henry, drawing a moral shadow across the very keenness the other witnesses simply admire.

So the witnesses converge on the wonder and part only in its use. Gill, Clarke, and Wesley dwell on the sheer power of the eye that pierces from the cloud to the smallest creature hidden below, a faculty Job never gave and cannot rival; Henry alone bends it into a warning against the devout hunter of earthly prey. The divine speech, for its part, presses the plainer point: the eagle's telescopic sight, like her soaring and her fastness, is a work of God past all Job's contriving, one more instance in the long gallery of a wisdom lodged in the creatures that leaves the man who would reason with God with nothing of his own to plead. The far-seeing eye looks down upon a world it did not make, from a height its Maker alone appointed.
30:
The gallery ends where all flesh ends, at the field of the slain, and the eagle stoops to it: "Her young ones also suck up blood: and where the slain are, there is she." The reformed John Gill notes that the young suck up blood as well as the dam, being brought up to it; the eagle cares not for water but drinks the blood of her prey, and her young after her, as the naturalists report, while Aelianus says the same of the hawk, that it eats no seeds but devours flesh and drinks blood, and nourishes its young with the same. The wesleyan-arminian Adam Clarke adds that the eagle does not feed her young with carrion but with prey newly slain, that they may suck up the blood; and the closing clause, "where the slain are, there is she," he observes, was quoted by our Lord — "wheresoever the carcase is, there will the eagles be gathered together" in Matt. 24:28 — a likely proverbial saying which Christ adapted to the Jewish people, about to fall a prey to the Romans.

The grammatical-historical witnesses keep to the wording. Charles Ellicott simply compares the same clause with Matt. 24:28 and Luke 17:37; and Keil and Delitzsch render the couplet plainly, "and its young ones suck up blood, and where the slain are, there is it," letting the grim image close their strophe on the birds of prey.

The puritan-evangelical Matthew Henry draws the whole chapter to its rest in this last figure. The eagle preys upon living animals, which she seizes and tears and carries to her young, that are taught to suck up blood; and she preys too upon the dead, for where the slain are, there is she — these birds, in another sense than the war-horse of v.25, smelling the battle afar off. So when a great slaughter is to be made among the enemies of the church, Henry notes, the fowls are invited to the supper of the great God in Rev. 19:17, and our Saviour himself refers to this instinct of the eagle. And these many instances of natural power and sagacity in the inferior creatures, which we cannot account for, oblige us, Henry concludes, to confess our own weakness and ignorance and to give glory to God as the fountain of all being, power, wisdom, and perfection. The witnesses do not divide; they close the gallery of the wild on the eagle over the carcase, and gather the whole procession of goat and ass and wild ox, of ostrich and horse and hawk, into one confession — that the God who feeds even the eaglets on blood in the clefts of the rock rules a world so far beyond Job's knowing that the only answer left to him is silence and worship.
